account: Chicago's Department of Innovation and Technology and Department of Public Health built a model. Pro bono data scientists from Allstate Insurance and the Civic Consulting Alliance helped. It assigns each of the city's 15,000+ food establishments a likelihood of a critical violation. Predictors include previous critical or serious violations, three-day average high temperature, nearby garbage and sanitation complaints and facility type. Others are nearby burglaries, licenses, time since last inspection, length of operation and the inspector assigned. In a double-blind retrodiction, the Department of Public Health inspected 1,637 establishments in its normal order during September and October 2014. Of these, 258 (almost 16%) had at least one critical violation, and 141 of those (55%) were found in the first month. Re-ordering the same inspections by the model's probabilities would have found 178 (69%) in the first half of the work, on average 7.5 days earlier. Another 37 would have been cited in the first month. The Department of Public Health began using the model in January 2015. On 19 May 2015 the Harvard Ash Center's Data-Smart City Solutions published an article on the pilot. The city's own page on the pilot is undated, and the code is open source in R. In a 2019 analysis, independent researchers at the Illinois Institute of Technology re-ran the city's simulation and found an average gain of 7.4 days, with a standard deviation of 25 days. They also found that the strongest predictor was the group of inspectors who last visited. They report that the rise in violation rates after 2015 cannot be shown to come from the model.

ai_role.statement: The model is a logistic regression built by the City of Chicago with pro bono partners and used by the Department of Public Health to order inspections; inspectors carry out every inspection. An independent re-run confirms the simulated gain of about 7.4 days, with a standard deviation of 25.2 days. The same analysis found that the most influential feature was the group of inspectors who last visited an establishment, and its authors argue that this feature unfairly raises risk scores. The authors could not separate the model's effect in live use from restaurant turnover and stricter inspection after improved training.

fields.account: Chicago's Department of Innovation and Technology and Department of Public Health built a model. Pro bono data scientists from Allstate Insurance and the Civic Consulting Alliance helped. It assigns each of the city's 15,000+ food establishments a likelihood of a critical violation. Predictors include previous critical or serious violations, three-day average high temperature, nearby garbage and sanitation complaints and facility type. Others are nearby burglaries, licenses, time since last inspection, length of operation and the inspector assigned. In a double-blind retrodiction, the Department of Public Health inspected 1,637 establishments in its normal order during September and October 2014. Of these, 258 (almost 16%) had at least one critical violation, and 141 of those (55%) were found in the first month. Re-ordering the same inspections by the model's probabilities would have found 178 (69%) in the first half of the work, on average 7.5 days earlier. Another 37 would have been cited in the first month. The Department of Public Health began using the model in January 2015. On 19 May 2015 the Harvard Ash Center's Data-Smart City Solutions published an article on the pilot. The city's own page on the pilot is undated, and the code is open source in R. In a 2019 analysis, independent researchers at the Illinois Institute of Technology re-ran the city's simulation and found an average gain of 7.4 days, with a standard deviation of 25 days. They also found that the strongest predictor was the group of inspectors who last visited. They report that the rise in violation rates after 2015 cannot be shown to come from the model.

purpose: Forecast which Chicago food establishments are most likely to have critical sanitation violations so that inspectors visit them first.

ratings.reason: The sources document a retrospective simulation, in which 69% of the establishments with critical violations would have been found in the first half of the work against 55% in the normal order. No source documents an outcome of live use that can be attributed to the model.
The sources give earlier discovery of violations as the rationale, since discovery otherwise may come “potentially after patrons became ill”. No source documents an outcome for illness.
